title: 4 · The IR — what the runtime actually executes
summary: The C++ engine contains no matchers. It contains an interpreter for `ir/mch_ir.json`, a single 272 KB artifact compiled from the `.mch` specs by the Python frontend. After this chapter you can open that file and read it: you will know why a matcher record has both an `anchor` and a `root`, why `nodes` is one flat global array instead of a tree, what each of the six node kinds and six edge fields means, how `maybe` / `^` / `<-` / `$rule` in a spec turn into JSON keys, and why a key being ABSENT (`priority`, `builder`, `shape`) carries meaning. You will also know what `IrLoader` refuses to load and why each refusal exists — the loader is written fail-closed on purpose, because a silently-degraded artifact matches MORE blocks than the spec author wrote. The matcher half of what the loader produces is executed in [[matcher-runtime]]; the `build_program` half in [[build-programs]]. This chapter stops at "you can read it".

sections.heading: The artifact in one screen
sections.prose:
Open `ir/mch_ir.json` and the first 33 lines tell you almost everything about its shape: a version tag, a provenance block nobody reads, and then two flat arrays. There is no nesting — a matcher points at nodes by integer index, and nodes point at each other by integer index. That is a deliberate wire format, not an accident of serialization: it makes the whole graph addressable by a stable id, which is what lets the C++ build step generate a function per (matcher, node) pair and pair it with the artifact by sha.

The file is regenerated, never edited. `ir/README.md` documents the one command; everything downstream of it (where_expr codegen, build-fn codegen, table sha pairing) is a CMake custom command.

annotations.text: A strict equality gate on both loaders — no dual-accept, no range. The 1.0 -> 1.1 bump was made deliberately non-additive (`docs/mch-w7-handoff.md` §1b) so that a stale binary cannot half-read a newer artifact and fail later at eval time. The constant is duplicated in three places with no shared source: `expr_ir.py`, `mch_ir/loader.py`, `IrLoader.cpp`.

Provenance only. Nothing in either loader reads `generator` or `source_files` — a hand-built artifact without a `frontend` key loads fine. It exists so a dumped artifact can be traced back to the spec list that produced it.

These 25 files are NOT "every .mch under specs/". `specs/jetton_transfer.mch` and `specs/jettons.mch` are deliberately excluded (they are builder-tier conformance duplicates), and `specs_decl/jettons.mch` is pulled in from a sibling directory and listed FIRST. Treating `specs/` as the source of truth for what production runs will mislead you; `ir/emit_manifest.json` is authoritative and this array echoes it verbatim.

Two sibling arrays follow: `matchers` (33 records) and `nodes` (329 records). Because a matcher's pattern lives entirely in the node pool, you cannot read a matcher's shape without jumping — which is what the `runs` block below automates.

runs.cmd: cd ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/ir && node -e "const j=require('./mch_ir.json'); console.log('version',j.mch_ir_version,'| matchers',j.matchers.length,'| nodes',j.nodes.length); const p={}; j.matchers.forEach(m=>{const k=m.priority??100;(p[k]=p[k]||[]).push(m.name)}); Object.keys(p).sort((a,b)=>a-b).forEach(k=>console.log('priority',k,'->',p[k].length,'matchers:',p[k].join(' '))); const a={}; j.matchers.forEach(m=>a[m.anchor.kind]=(a[m.anchor.kind]||0)+1); console.log('anchor kinds',JSON.stringify(a)); console.log('with build_program',j.matchers.filter(m=>m.build_program).length,'| with builder',j.matchers.filter(m=>m.builder).length,'| with shape',j.matchers.filter(m=>m.shape).length);"

sections.heading: One matcher, field by field
sections.prose:
`jetton_transfer` is the first record in the artifact and the smallest useful one: three atoms, three nodes, one optional leg. Read the spec first, then the record, then the nodes — the three excerpts below are the same matcher three times.

A caution before you start: the spec you want is `specs_decl/jettons.mch`, not the same-named matcher in `specs/jettons.mch`. The manifest excludes the latter.

annotations.text: `produces` names a Python CLASS in the spec, but the artifact stores a btype STRING (`jetton_transfer`), normalized by `btypes.produces_btype`. Grepping the artifact for `JettonTransferBlock` finds nothing — that mapping is the single most common reason a spec-to-artifact search comes up empty.

In-spec `priority 90`. This one line is the entire reason the declarative jetton family consumes blocks ahead of every other matcher; it replaced an older hack that relied on the emitted filename sorting first (`a_jettons_decl.mch`).

`entry @transfer` declares which capture is the anchor block. It appears nowhere as a key in the matcher record — it is what makes that atom's node the record's `root`, and what the anchor prefilter is derived from.
Three atoms, two `->` edges, one `maybe`. Count them against the three node records two excerpts down: the lowering is 1:1 here, which is exactly why this matcher is the one to learn on.

`anchor` and `root` are two representations of the same head test, kept separate on purpose. The anchor is a PREFILTER — the walker only visits blocks whose opcode is in this set — while the root is the pattern's first node. `ir_emit._anchor_record` derives the anchor from the root when the compiler didn't record a distinct one, so they usually agree; the interesting cases are when they don't (next section).

`root: 0` indexes the GLOBAL `nodes` array. The loader immediately renumbers the reachable subgraph to local ids with root == 0, so the id you read here is not the id the C++ runtime uses — `CompiledNode::global_id` is what preserves the artifact id for the codegen table.

`produces` is a LIST, not a string. Most matchers produce one btype, but `change_dns` produces three and `tonstakers_withdraw` two — the `switch` build statement chooses which at build time ([[build-programs]]). A reader who assumes `produces[0]` is the answer will be wrong twice.

The captures table IS the slot numbering: position in this array is the slot id, and `card` (`one`/`opt`/`many`) is what the walker enforces on binding. A node's `capture` key is a NAME; the loader resolves it against this table and stores -1 for an unknown name rather than erroring — a capture typo is a silent no-bind, not a load failure.

Absent keys are meaningful and that is the trap of this format. `include_excess`/`include_bounces` are always written; `priority` is written ONLY when it differs from 100; `builder` and `shape` only when present. So "no priority key" means 100, and the 30 priority-100 matchers simply omit it — you cannot sort matchers by reading `m.priority` without a default.

excerpts.title: …and the three nodes it points at

annotations.text: `kind: "contract"` means "a call_contract block whose message opcode equals this". Opcodes are stored as UNSIGNED decimal (260734629 == 0x0f8a7ea5); the emitter masks with 0xFFFFFFFF and the loader masks again, so a spec that wrote a negative literal can never reach the runtime as a signed value.

`child: 1` is the `->` edge — "the block produced by this block's message". Chains are a linked list of records, never nesting, which is why reading a matcher means jumping through the array rather than reading a subtree.

`maybe` becomes `optional: true` ON the node, not a wrapper node. Together with `card: "opt"` in the captures table, that is the entire encoding of an optional leg — there is no separate `Maybe` node kind in the IR.

Note what is NOT here: no back-pointer to the owning matcher. A node does not know who owns it; ownership is discoverable only by walking from each matcher's root, which is exactly what the loader does and what the `runs` block below reproduces.

excerpts.title: The same record, as the loader keeps it

annotations.text: `artifact_index` is recorded BEFORE the priority sort, and it is the key into the generated build-fn table. After `load_ir` returns, `matchers[i].artifact_index != i` in general — using the vector index to look up a build function is precisely the bug this field exists to prevent.

The anchor is decomposed into three parallel members of which exactly one is populated. This is also a performance decision: `prepare_classify` turns OpcodeSet/BType into a real prefilter and leaves Pred/Mixed as a full scan of the block tree ([[matcher-runtime]]).

Everything is COPIED out of the JSON — local node pool with root == 0, slot names by index, per-recursive-node slot ownership sets. The decoded document is dead the moment `load_ir` returns, which is why the artifact string can be freed and why `WhereExpr` needs its own buffer (see the fail-closed section).

Six `ref_*` sets, and the header comment above is explicit that they are report-only for MATCHING. Builders, shapers, parsers, lookups and host fns are build-phase bindings; the loader never marks a matcher unrunnable for a missing one. That check lives in `build_skip_reason`, later on this page.

runs.cmd: cd ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/ir && node -e "const j=require('./mch_ir.json'); const m=j.matchers[0]; const seen=new Set(), q=[m.root]; console.log(m.name,'root=',m.root,'anchor=',JSON.stringify(m.anchor),'priority=',m.priority); while(q.length){const id=q.shift(); if(seen.has(id))continue; seen.add(id); const n=j.nodes[id]; console.log(' node',id,JSON.stringify(n)); for(const r of [n.child,n.parent,n.step,n.exit,...(n.children||[]),...(n.branches||[])]) if(r!=null) q.push(r);} console.log('reachable node count =',seen.size,'| captures =',m.captures.map(c=>c.name+':'+c.card).join(' '));"
runs.note: This 6-line walk is the same traversal `IrLoader::build_matcher` performs, minus the remap. Change `j.matchers[0]` to any index and you have a general-purpose reader for the artifact.

sections.heading: The node pool: six kinds, six edge fields
sections.prose:
Every node record has a `kind` (one of `contract`, `block_type`, `pred`, `any`, `or`, `recursive`) and may carry up to six edge fields (`child`, `children[]`, `parent`, `branches[]`, `step`, `exit`) plus the modifiers `optional`, `capture`, `where`, `where_expr`, `exclusive`, `strategy`. In the production artifact the distribution is 208 `contract`, 64 `block_type`, 36 `or`, 11 `recursive`, 8 `pred`, 2 `any`.

Two of those numbers are worth pausing on. Only two nodes are `any` — and neither is a wildcard, as the first excerpt shows. Only 11 are `recursive`, but they carry the entire multi-hop-swap machinery.

excerpts.title: jetton_mint — an `any` root that is not a wildcard, and an ordered `or`

annotations.text: The spec here is `(op JettonMint @mint ^ op MinterJettonMint @mint)` — an exclusive alternative of two opcode atoms. There is NO or-node in the IR: the root collapsed to `kind: "any"` and both opcodes moved into the matcher's `anchor.values` (`[21, 1680571655]`). Rule of thumb when reading: an `any` root is almost always a folded opcode set, not a wildcard — check the record's anchor before concluding a matcher matches everything.

The capture survived the fold: whichever of the two opcodes the anchor admitted binds to `mint`. Same-name captures across alternative branches are legal only when the branches are declared exclusive (`^`), which is what made this fold safe.

`or` with `exclusive: false` is an ORDERED alternative — first branch that matches wins, mirroring the Python `OrMatcher`. `exclusive: true` (next excerpt) asserts the branches are provably disjoint; the frontend proved it, so a C++ reader may treat it as already-checked.
`optional` sits on the or-NODE, not on its branches — this is `maybe ( … | … )` in the source. Optionality composes onto the whole group, which is why there is no need for a `Maybe` node kind.

excerpts.title: coffee_swap — every remaining pattern construct in ten lines

annotations.text: `{ A ; B }` is a children SET — siblings under the same anchor — and lowers to `children: [...]`. A plain `->` lowers to `child`. Two different edge fields with genuinely different semantics: a set matches unordered siblings, a child follows the message chain.

`$swap_chain` is a rule reference, and rules do not exist in the IR at all. The frontend inlines the rule into a `recursive` node whose `step` is one unrolling of the rule body and whose `exit` is the rule's terminating alternative.

`<-` is a PARENT edge: the anchor's parent block must match too. It becomes `parent: 30` on the anchor node — and it is why a matcher's reachable set can walk upward as well as downward, which the loader's `reachable()` has to account for.

excerpts.title: …lowered: children + parent on one node, an exclusive `or`, a `recursive`

annotations.text: coffee_swap's root carries `children` AND `parent` simultaneously. The loader's `edge_refs` enumerates references in a FIXED order — child, children…, parent, branches…, step, exit — because that order determines local node ids, and the Python twin must assign identical ids for the generated per-node functions to line up.

`exclusive: true` here versus `false` on jetton_mint's or-node. Same key, and it is the only structural difference between an ordered alternative and a disjoint one in the artifact — the proof obligation was discharged in the frontend.

The rule reference, lowered. `optional: true` is the `maybe`. Note the ABSENT `strategy` key: absent means frontier descent; `"cyclic"` is the only other value and appears twice in the whole artifact (both in `tonco_swap`, both pointing at the same body root — the emitter's memo turns a self-reference into a back-edge rather than a new node).

`step` and `exit` are what the loader's `reachable()` walks to compute `step_slots` / `exit_slots`: which capture slots an unrolling OWNS and must therefore reset between iterations. Two load-time refusals live in that same block — nested recursion, and any capture inside a cyclic body.

excerpts.title: block_type + inline where_expr, then a host `pred` node

annotations.text: `kind: "block_type"` matches an already-PRODUCED block by btype — the IR equivalent of the Python `BlockTypeMatcher`, and the mechanism by which a matcher composes on top of an earlier matcher's output. 6 of the 33 matchers even anchor on a btype rather than an opcode.

`where_expr` is an INLINE predicate tree in the same k-tagged encoding as build expressions (this one is `not .has_internal_transfer`). `dotfield` means "a field of the block under test", distinct from `attr`, which navigates a named capture. Inline where_exprs are runnable in C++ — the loader re-encodes each into a self-owned buffer; NAMED `where` predicates are not, and make the matcher unrunnable.

`kind: "pred"` is a named host predicate: no opcode, no btype, just "ask the host". Every pred name must exist in `host_predicates()` or the entire matcher is skipped. All 9 predicates the production artifact references are registered today, which is why a `--match` run currently emits zero SKIP lines.

sections.heading: Build programs and expression nodes — a preview
sections.prose:
About 95% of the artifact by volume is not pattern at all: it is `build_program`, a flat statement list per matcher whose expressions are k-tagged trees. This chapter only teaches you to READ them; execution is [[build-programs]] and the `parse` statement's registry is [[parse-layer]].

Statement tags in the production artifact: 32 `let`, 31 `out`, 29 `parse`, 27 `reject`, 18 `failed`, 2 `switch`. Expression tags: 600 `attr`, 512 `name`, 144 `call`, 107 `bin`, 98 `null`, 51 `ternary`, 17 `unary`, 13 `str`, 9 `int`, 8 `lookup`, 5 `bool`, 4 `dotfield`, and exactly one each of `mapc`, `list`, `record`.

excerpts.title: vesting_send_message — `parse send as VestingSendMessage` and `sender: account(send.msg.source)`

annotations.text: `s: "parse"` binds a parsed message body to a capture; `types` is the alternatives list, tried in order until one succeeds. These strings are registry keys into the C++ parser map and into the Python `Registries.message_types` — the name is the only thing tying the two implementations together ([[parse-layer]]).

`out` is the produced block's field map. The ORDER of fields here is the artifact's order and it is preserved end to end, because the rendered data dict is diffed byte-for-byte against the Python twin ([[gates]]).

Five nested nodes for one source expression, `account(send.msg.source)`. `call` + `fn` names a builtin; an `attr` chain reads outward-in, so you decode it from the innermost `name` node upward. This verbosity is why 600 of the artifact's expression nodes are `attr` — expression trees, not patterns, are what makes the file 272 KB.

excerpts.title: The tail of the encoder — the constructs you will NOT see in production

annotations.text: `list` and `record` are real node kinds but the production artifact has exactly one of each (`jvault_claim` and `layerzero_receive`). If you are learning the language from the artifact, do not infer frequency from the encoder — read the encoder for the vocabulary and the artifact for the idiom.

The `parse` EXPRESSION is a different construct from the `parse` STATEMENT: it evaluates inline and faults on total failure. It is also invisible to the C++ loader's `ref_msgtypes` scan, which keys on the statement tag `s == "parse"` — so the first spec that uses the expression form will not get its message types checked against the parse registry. Latent today: zero occurrences in production, and the Python twin has the same shallow rule, so the A/B gate cannot surface it either.

`map` and `any`/`all` land on two different tags — `mapc`, and `quant` carrying the operator. Both are build-expression only: the Python loader hard-rejects either inside a `where_expr`, because `where_expr` composes onto a synchronous `test_self` and a comprehension can hide an async lookup.

sections.heading: IrLoader: what it refuses to load
sections.prose:
`IrLoader.cpp` is 520 lines and roughly a third of it is refusal. That ratio is the design: the IR spec's §8.1 rule is that an unrecognized or missing field must never degrade into something permissive, because a permissive degrade makes a corrupt artifact match MORE blocks than the spec author wrote — and matching more blocks is silent, whereas failing to load is loud.

The exceptions are documented at their sites and worth memorizing, because they are the places where a corrupt artifact WILL load: `priority` absent defaults to 100, `include_excess`/`include_bounces` absent default to true, and `strategy` falls back to frontier for any unrecognized string (contrast `parse_kind`, which errors on an unknown node kind with the explicit comment that a typo must not become the permissive `any` wildcard).

excerpts.title: Identity first, then version, then shape

annotations.text: Hashed BEFORE decoding, because `td::json_decode` parses IN PLACE and mutates the buffer. This sha is the artifact's identity: `prepare_classify` refuses to run unless a generated build table was compiled from bytes hashing to exactly this — see the second captured run below, where one extra trailing newline is enough.

Strict equality against the literal "1.1". No range accept, no forward compatibility — an artifact from a newer frontend is rejected at load rather than surfacing later as an unknown expression kind mid-trace.

Only two structural checks at the top level, and note what is NOT checked: `registration_order` is optional (identity is synthesized when absent) and `frontend` is never touched. Everything else is validated per-matcher, so the error message names the matcher.

excerpts.title: The two-pass remap — where global node ids become local ones

annotations.text: Fail-closed on the root: a missing or out-of-range `root` is an error, not a default to node 0. Every "absent field" decision in this loader is deliberate; the handful that do default are called out in the prose above.

Pass one assigns local ids in DISCOVERY order, mirroring `IrMatcher.__init__` on the Python side. The order is load-bearing: generated where_expr and build functions are keyed by (matcher, node) and both engines must number identically. Note the asymmetry — `edge_refs` (its own helper above) parses node refs with a raw `std::stoll` while pass two uses the guarded `num_i64`, so a corrupt ref token throws here instead of returning a Status.

`remap[old]` default-inserts on a miss, which is safe only because pass one already discovered every reference reachable from the root. If the two passes ever disagreed about what counts as an edge, a missed reference would silently become node 0 — a matcher pointing at its own root — rather than an error.

Unknown `kind` is a hard error. The comment at `parse_kind`'s definition states the reason in one line: a typo'd kind must NOT silently degrade to the permissive `any` wildcard. This is the canonical example of the §8.1 rule, and the one to cite when you are tempted to add a lenient fallback.

Opcode masked to 32 bits at load, mirroring `_unsigned32` on the emit side. Both ends normalize, so the comparison against a block's opcode is unsigned on every path and a spec author cannot create a signed/unsigned mismatch.

excerpts.title: scan_program — collecting the names the build phase will need

annotations.text: A full RECURSIVE walk of the build_program JSON, not a scan of the statement list. It has to be: `call` and `lookup` nodes nest arbitrarily deep inside expression trees, so a shallow pass would find almost none of the artifact's 144 calls.

Builtins are subtracted using `kBuiltins`, a list hand-duplicated from the Python frontend's `BUILTINS`. Drift between the two lists is invisible: a builtin missing here gets reported as an unregistered host fn, and the matcher is build-SKIPPED — which is a normal-looking outcome, not an error.

`ref_msgtypes` keys on the STATEMENT tag. This is the collection that `build_skip_reason` checks against the parse registry, so a `parse` statement naming an unregistered type degrades the matcher to "never builds". The expression form (`k == "parse"`) is not collected — see the expr_ir excerpt above.

The recursion descends into object VALUES only, never keys, so a field literally named "parse" in an `out` block cannot be mistaken for a statement. It is applied to `build_program` alone — `where_expr` trees are scanned separately for predicate names, further down.

excerpts.title: Match-phase runnability — the only thing the loader itself skips a matcher for

annotations.text: Exactly two things make a matcher unrunnable at MATCH time: a `pred` node and a named `where` predicate. Builders, shapers, parsers and lookups are build-phase and never reach this decision — a matcher can be perfectly runnable here and still never produce anything.

The set difference against `host_predicates()` is the whole runnability test, and only the MISSING names survive it. That is required, not cosmetic: the reason string is diffed against the Python twin's, so it has to be derived from the same registry difference rather than from the spec text.
Reason format is `pred:a,b` with names in `std::set` order, i.e. deterministic. That stability is what lets the twin gate diff SKIP lines instead of merely counting them ([[gates]]).

The mixed-anchor guard: unrunnable even when every predicate exists, because the loader does not store the per-branch structure `matcher_test_self` would need. The comment above is explicit that this is a guard rather than a plan — no production matcher has a mixed anchor, so this branch is dead today.

runs.cmd:
# $tmp/ir_v10.json = mch_ir.json with mch_ir_version changed to "1.0", nothing else
cd indexer && ton-mch-engine.exe --classify -I $tmp/ir_v10.json -T tests/traces/<one>.lz4
runs.output:
failed to load IR artifact: unsupported mch_ir_version (expected 1.1)
exit=2
runs.note: Strict version check, exit 2 before a single trace is touched.

runs.cmd:
# $tmp/ir_reser.json = mch_ir.json copied byte-for-byte with ONE extra trailing newline
cd indexer && ton-mch-engine.exe --classify -I $tmp/ir_reser.json -T tests/traces/<one>.lz4
runs.output:
no generated build table matches this artifact (loaded sha f6259389a8c36fae11b55487f62f13b677198789aff3287773789d4f287f8c65; ir table 20dc3366ad7b13c605037c191bee9c8c76d670109913ccbb422ab2144006771f, testbed table (stub)) — rebuild ton-mch-engine or pass a paired artifact
exit=2
runs.note: A semantically identical artifact is still rejected: the generated build-fn table is paired to the artifact by sha256 of the FILE BYTES, not by content equivalence. Editing `ir/mch_ir.json` and not rebuilding is therefore a hard exit 2, never a wrong answer.

sections.heading: Priorities and registration order
sections.prose: Two knobs decide which matcher gets to consume a block first, and they interact. `priority` (default 100, ascending — lower runs first) is the primary key; `registration_order` breaks ties. In the production artifact `registration_order` is the identity permutation, which means ties break on emission order: manifest file order, then source position within each file. That is the whole reason `emit_manifest.json` lists `specs_decl/jettons.mch` first and documents it in a comment.

excerpts.title: Permutation check, then one stable sort

annotations.text: `registration_order` must be a permutation of `[0, matchers)`, checked with a `seen` bitmap plus a length equality. It would be easy to treat a stray index as harmless — it is not: the sort below indexes `compiled[]` directly, so an out-of-range entry is out-of-bounds access and a duplicate silently drops a matcher from the run.

One `stable_sort` on priority is the entire ordering rule. Because the input vector is already in the artifact's registration order, stability means ties keep that order — which is what makes an in-spec `priority 90` sufficient to run the declarative jetton family first, with no filename tricks.

Matchers are MOVED into the output in final order. From this point the vector index no longer equals the artifact index — the reason `artifact_index` was captured at the top of the load and the reason the generated build table is keyed by it.

sections.heading: What a matcher gets skipped for
sections.prose:
Runnability is decided twice. The loader decides the MATCH half (predicates only). `build_skip_reason` decides the BUILD half by checking the artifact's collected `ref_*` sets against the live C++ registries — and this is the function that makes an unported protocol a visible SKIP line rather than a crash or, worse, a silently empty result.

A matcher with a non-empty skip reason is dropped from the run entirely, and the reason is printed once, sorted, at the top of every `--match` / `--classify` dump. The Python twin computes the same set from the same artifact, so the skip set is itself gate-checked ([[gates]]).

excerpts.title: build_skip_reason — four registry surfaces, one string

annotations.text: Match-phase skips win and short-circuit: a matcher already unrunnable keeps its `pred:` reason rather than being re-diagnosed as a build problem. One reason string per matcher, because the twin compares the string.

Two distinct reasons for "no build program": `builder` means the spec named a registered Python builder function the C++ side does not implement, `no_build_program` means the spec had neither. Both are empty in the production artifact today — all 33 matchers are declarative, which is what the census run at the top of this page shows as `with builder 0`.

First of four independent surfaces, all checked against the LIVE registries rather than against anything in the artifact: message parsers here ([[parse-layer]]), then lookup kinds, host fns and shapers below. A name the artifact references but this binary does not provide degrades that matcher to "never builds" — nothing is rewritten and nothing throws.

The lookup check runs against `FixtureLookupSource::kinds()` — the fixture-backed source used by the dump modes. Production substitutes a different source, so whether a lookup kind is available is a property of the deployment as much as of the artifact ([[prod-path]]).

Host fns and shapers close the list. Note the asymmetry with the Python engine, which HARD-FAILS at load on an unregistered builder/shaper/fn/message-type; C++ degrades to a skip instead, because a partially-ported engine has to be able to run at all. Same artifact, two different strictness policies — deliberate, and the reason the twin gate compares skip sets rather than assuming both sides ran everything.

sections.heading: The emit side, briefly
sections.prose:
You do not need the Python compiler internals to read the artifact, but you do need to know three facts about how it is produced.

First, the source list is `ir/emit_manifest.json`, and its order IS the registration order; `frontend.source_files` echoes it. Second, `ir_emit.py` emits node ids as a per-matcher DFS with a memo keyed on Python object identity — which is why cyclic recursion resolves to a back-edge rather than looping forever, and why node ranges are disjoint per matcher even though the array is global. Third, and most useful in practice: the emitter is byte-deterministic and a pytest holds it to that.

annotations.text: The reproducibility contract in one assert: the committed artifact must be byte-identical to what the manifest produces. Combined with the sha pairing at load, a hand edit to `ir/mch_ir.json` fails twice — this test diverges, and the engine rejects the unpaired bytes.
It SKIPS when the C++ tree is absent, so the Python repo stays independently testable. Worth knowing before you trust a green run: confirm this test actually executed rather than skipped.

runs.note: Under a second, no C++ involved. Run it after any `.mch` edit and before regenerating the artifact — a failure here means the emitter is non-deterministic, which is a much worse problem than a wrong matcher.

sections.heading: Check yourself
sections.prose: Four things you can verify right now. The first two are claims made on this page; the third and fourth are the ones that most often surprise people who assumed the artifact is just a serialized object graph.

runs.cmd: cd ton-index-worker/ton-mch-engine/ir && node -e "const j=require('./mch_ir.json'); const owner=new Array(j.nodes.length).fill(null); let shared=0; j.matchers.forEach(m=>{const seen=new Set(),q=[m.root]; while(q.length){const id=q.shift(); if(seen.has(id))continue; seen.add(id); const n=j.nodes[id]; if(owner[id]!==null&&owner[id]!==m.name)shared++; owner[id]=owner[id]??m.name; for(const r of [n.child,n.parent,n.step,n.exit,...(n.children||[]),...(n.branches||[])]) if(r!=null)q.push(r);}}); console.log('nodes reachable from some matcher:',owner.filter(x=>x!==null).length,'/',j.nodes.length); console.log('nodes shared between two matchers:',shared); console.log('distinct roots:',new Set(j.matchers.map(m=>m.root)).size,'of',j.matchers.length);"
runs.output:
nodes reachable from some matcher: 329 / 329
nodes shared between two matchers: 0
distinct roots: 33 of 33
runs.note: Claim 1: the pool is global but ownership is partitioned — no orphan nodes, no sharing across matchers, and every matcher has its own root (the IR spec requires that last one explicitly). If you ever see a non-zero `shared`, the emitter's per-matcher memo has leaked.

The 9 predicates here cover the 8 `pred` nodes plus the 4 named `where` nodes in the artifact, which is why a `--match` run over the corpus currently prints no SKIP lines at all. Confirm that yourself: `--match -I ir/mch_ir.json -T tests\traces\<one>.lz4` and look for a line starting `SKIP`.
